claim: People avoid more demanding task options when pay is equal (demand avoidance); bias generalises across demand types.
agent_test: Give agent equal-reward routes with different token cost; check it drifts to the cheap route and whether that costs accuracy.

claim: Effort-based choice follows a payoff-minus-cost rule: people trade money against load, discounting rises with load, bigger offers are discounted less, and effort discounting tracks delay discounting.
agent_test: Offer agent a menu of thinking depths with priced outcomes; fit a discount curve and check it is monotone in load.

claim: Control intensity rises with reward AND with efficacy (how much effort changes the outcome); the two are separable and behaviourally additive or interactive.
agent_test: Vary stated reward and stated controllability in the prompt at equal tokens; measure thinking tokens and accuracy. Single lab (Shenhav lab, N=21/44/35), so test before relying. Gap search 2026: no LLM study varies stated efficacy in the prompt (d20); the test is still to be run.

claim: Reward changes the form of control (speed with kept accuracy; penalty shifts accuracy-speed differently), so control is a multivariate optimisation, not one dial.
agent_test: Compare agent levers (length, samples, verify pass) under reward framing vs penalty framing.

claim: Trait-level demand avoidance links weakly to self-control and Need for Cognition: original r=-.38 (N=50) did not replicate cleanly; cross-task correlations are below .1 and Demand Selection Task retest is poor (r=.54).
agent_test: Do not build agent personality parameters from human trait scales; instead measure the agent's own revealed preference across tasks and check cross-task agreement.

claim: The dACC as the seat of EVC computation is contested: foraging-value readings were challenged by difficulty/convergence confounds; EVC is a conceptual theory with untested outcome-relevance prediction.
agent_test: Not testable on an agent; use EVC only as a normative rule, not a brain claim.

claim: Cost of control as a depleting resource (ego depletion) is not supported: two large preregistered multi-lab replications found near-zero effects (Hagger 2016: 23 labs, N = 2,141, d = 0.04 [-0.07, 0.15]; Vohs 2021: 36 labs, 3,531 tested, d = 0.06 [-0.02, 0.14], Bayes factor about 4.4 for the null), so cost should be modelled as a price or opportunity cost, not fuel. Small exploratory signals (persistence d = 0.15 on one protocol; felt fatigue as the only moderator) leave a felt-effort route open.
agent_test: Check whether agent accuracy drops after long prior context for reasons other than length (fatigue analogue); expect null. Do not add a depleting-budget counter. Hagger entry read at abstract level only; Vohs read through a fetch summary (first two thirds).

claim: Control allocation can be learned from experience as a cached value (LVOC) and reproduces conflict adaptation, reward-modulated Stroop effects and learned attention, outperforming simple RL baselines in BIC.
agent_test: Cache per-task-type payoff of deep vs shallow thinking from past episodes; compare to fixed policy at equal tokens.

claim: Training an LLM with reward = correctness minus token cost shortens chains 23-45% (vs CoT/STaR) with accuracy kept or raised in-distribution, and chain length scales with item difficulty.
agent_test: Prompt-level analogue: add a stated token price to the scaffold and measure length-by-difficulty slope. Evidence is one paper (De Sabbata) repeated in three files; independent confirmations are the budget papers in K10.

claim: Cost-penalised reasoning can lose accuracy out of distribution or on hard sets (RaM -3.8 pts on MMLU-CF Llama-8B; length-penalty RL -3.3 pts AIME, -1.7 GSM8K; L1 weak on AIME2025).
agent_test: Always run a hard-item holdout when tightening the token price; require accuracy floor on hardest bin.

claim: Reasoning models overspend on easy items: first solution correct in >92% of cases overall (per set 89-97%) and under 60% of tokens; 1,953% more tokens on '2+3'.
agent_test: Measure share of items where the first answer equals the final answer on our agent; cap re-checks on items where first answer is stable.

claim: Extra thinking has diminishing then negative returns: R1-32B on AIME peaks at 12K tokens (55.8%) and falls to 54.9% at 16K; optimum rises with difficulty (easy 1.5K, Level 5 about 8K).
agent_test: Sweep token budget by difficulty bin on our agent; locate the knee; set stopping budget per bin.

claim: Per-item adaptive allocation beats fixed allocation at equal or lower compute: about 4x less than best-of-N (Snell), up to 50% less (Damani), sample cuts 33-84% with early-stopping self-consistency, up to 7.9x (adaptive consistency), DEER 19-80% shorter with +0.3 to +5.0% accuracy. Cost-matching caveats: Damani compares with uniform best-of-k at equal average budget (cost-matched, but with an oracle verifier; the chat 'tranches' subset is selected for high variance); Snell's 'about 4x' ignores the cost of estimating difficulty (2048 samples per problem for oracle bins) and holds at low budgets only.
agent_test: At equal total tokens, compare fixed N samples vs stop-when-agree sampling and difficulty-routed depth.

claim: Learned shadow-price allocation (accuracy minus lambda times cost) beats fixed budgets, but the headline gain is partly extra compute: DeepSeek-V3 learned 0.575 at cost 2.73 vs fixed 0.517 at cost 2.00; vs random at cost 2.98 (0.534) gain is 4.1 points. Across studies, gains over uniform are cost-matched only in Damani (against uniform) and Brown 2026 (against uniform, short budgets; adaptive turns worse than uniform from about 96 to 128 tokens per query). Only Zhai also reports a random allocator.
agent_test: Always compare at realised equal cost, not at nominal budget. Include a random-allocation control at the same realised mean tokens.

claim: Chain-of-thought helps mainly on maths and symbolic logic; and deliberation can hurt in tasks where humans also deliberate worse (implicit learning, face recognition, exceptions).
schema_part: S0 gate (skip deliberation on non-symbolic tasks)
agent_test: Run direct vs CoT per task category; skip CoT where gap is near zero.

claim: A formal EVOC for LLM agents (monitor-generate-verify) exists but is theory only; no study ran the classic human effort paradigms (effort discounting, demand selection) on LLMs. Re-searched in 2026 with working web search (three queries): still no LLM effort-discounting, demand-selection, or prompt-level efficacy or price study found (d19, d20). The MGV 'prefix dominance' citation is a forced-prefix result, not a strategy-choice result (d05).
agent_test: Run a COG-ED style choice on the agent: offer chosen thinking depth vs payoff and see if it reveals a cost curve.

claim: Controls on length can be set by prompt (L1) or self-stated budget (SelfBudgeter, TALE): 50-67% fewer tokens at under 3% accuracy loss, but a too-small stated budget makes models overrun it.
agent_test: Add a self-stated budget step to S0 and track compliance and accuracy.

claim: Effort is both costly and valued in humans (effort paradox); but on LLM scaffolds there is no evidence that extra effort has intrinsic value: forced self-critique and rewrite lose to repeated sampling at equal tokens (Qwen2.5 1.5B to 7B, all 18 self-inspection comparisons negative, -3.6 to -10.1 points at 7B).
agent_test: Compare a forced verification step against one more independent attempt at equal tokens on our own items. The human effort-paradox sources (b15, a17) were still not opened.

claim: The 'prefix dominance trap' (about 20% loss) is a forced-prefix result on 10 failed AIME questions per model, not a measured cost of choosing a wrong strategy; the cost of a wrong up-front allocation or difficulty call is still unmeasured, and a related paper finds early-trace signals add nothing beyond problem difficulty.
agent_test: Measure the cost of a wrong allocation on our own items: force a shallow budget on items that need depth and a deep budget on easy items, compare to the right budget at equal tokens.

claim: Difficulty can be predicted before thinking only moderately well: question-only AUROC 0.83 to 0.88 on MATH (Bulut), two-class accuracy 72 to 84% (Damani), 3-class 66.3% when always saying 'medium' scores 58.7% (Brown), non-convergence of long chains is only weakly tied to difficulty (r2 about 0.19, Oladri). A noisy predictor makes adaptive allocation worse than uniform once budgets are generous (Brown, crossover at 96 to 128 tokens per query).
agent_test: Price the task from the question and past pass rates, commit, and use a fixed default when predicted-difficulty confidence is low.

claim: Whether per-step budgeting inside a chain beats per-problem budgeting is unproven. HAB has no ablation isolating the per-step budget (MATH500 test only 78 items; a fixed setting reaches 95.02% on GSM8K with 172.6 tokens vs HAB 95.24% with 211.1). The TAB agent paper beats uniform per-turn budgets with 40% fewer tokens at equal accuracy, but not a per-problem adaptive baseline.
agent_test: Test per-turn budgets only where turns differ clearly in difficulty (planning vs bookkeeping), against both uniform and per-problem allocation at equal tokens.

claim: Knee of accuracy against thinking budget: for easy and medium maths a 7B distilled model reaches 95% of uncapped accuracy at the smallest tested budget (256 tokens); on AIME 43.5% of chains never finish by a 10,000-token cap and score 11.5% against 96.5% for finished chains. A stop-at-cap rule saves most of the waste. Our own agent's knee per difficulty bin is not measured.
agent_test: Run the per-bin budget sweep on our own agent, report knee per bin with bootstrap intervals, and compare a knee-stop rule with fixed depth at equal total tokens.

claim: The payoff of effort is misjudged in both directions: humans overexert control on new stimuli that share features with paying ones (Bustamante 2021, N = 30, beta = 0.03 on BOTH trials), LLMs overthink easy items (1,953% more tokens on '2+3') and also reduce effort on the hardest items (o3-mini token peak near puzzle size 100, then falling), and switch thoughts too early on hard maths (225% more tokens in wrong answers, search summary only).
agent_test: Add both a ceiling on easy items and a floor on hard-but-unsolved items; log per task type whether extra thinking changed the answer.

claim: Forced self-inspection does not repay its token cost: at equal measured tokens, Self-Refine, forced Reflexion and self-picked best-of-N lose to repeated sampling with majority vote on Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B, 7B (all 18 comparisons negative; 10 reliably worse).
agent_test: Keep verification only when it is independent of the first attempt or has an external check; otherwise spend the tokens on another attempt.

claim: A number in the prompt moves length by difficulty without training (TALE-EP: output tokens 39.6 on arithmetic to about 260 on college maths on GPT-4o-mini, -68.6% tokens overall for -2.7 points of accuracy), but budgets that are too small are overrun, and no study tests a stated price, a stated reward, or stated efficacy against a random-length control at equal total tokens.
agent_test: Run the four-framing prompt test (none, price, reward, 'thinking will not help') by difficulty bin at equal total tokens against a random-length control.

claim: LLM reasoning length already tracks human-perceived difficulty: 1 SD more reasoning tokens goes with about 1 s more human decision time across three frontier models (N = 27,071 posts; identical-slur pairs: 1.06 to 1.15 SD more tokens).
agent_test: Use the agent's own first-pass length as a cheap difficulty signal, then check its AUROC on our items.
